extracted.intended_audience: scholars and graduate students in philosophy and history of science studying models of scientific change
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether evolutionary (Darwinian/adaptive-walk) models adequately describe the historical development and normative features of scientific practice, and identifying the empirical/epistemic criteria such models must satisfy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foothold episodes as initiators of directional change
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial, often modest change (a 'foothold') gives a brief but highly resonant glimpse of a way forward and provides a foothold on a path that will eventuate in scientific achievement. Subsequent work is largely a campaign to bridge the gap between the foothold and the full achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'flash of brilliance' (but usually more modest), finding a really good research problem, Darwin's reading of Malthus, mathematical glimpses of proofs. The page emphasizes different species of footholds (problem selection, theoretical glimpses, methodological innovations, conceptual reconceptualizations) and warns not to over-emphasize rare brilliance flashes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nose for a good problem (criterion for scientific greatness)
rubrics_metrics.description: One quality that distinguishes great scientists is 'having a nose for a good problem' — an artistic ability to discern what is a good idea, what is a beautiful idea, what is worth spending time on, and, most importantly, what is a problem 'sufficiently interesting, yet sufficiently difficult that it hasn’t yet been solved, but the time for solving it has come now.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an evaluative standard for practitioners: selecting the right problem can be epoch-defining and strongly influences long-term productive trajectory; assessors should look for problem-choice that opens fruitful lines of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptive-walk pattern (big-to-small-to-smaller sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical development often follows an adaptive-walk signature: a grand initial step followed by relatively small movements whose reward depends on (1) their size and (2) how closely they remain on the path to the emerging optimum — i.e., a big-to-small-to-smaller pattern of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pattern is described as timescale-invariant and should be visible across scales (individual careers to field-level transitions). Use this pattern as an empirical expectation when testing whether scientific change conforms to a Darwinian/adaptive-walk model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological innovations functioning as footholds
rubrics_metrics.description: When practitioners face important problems with no apparent means of empirical resolution, methodological innovations (e.g., invention of the telescope) can provide the decisive foothold that enables rapid empirical progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate historical episodes for whether a single methodological step opened the way to resolve previously stalled problems; methodological innovation can be more decisive than early empirical results and often precipitates 'mop-up work' validating models' predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual reconceptualization that generates solvable problems
rubrics_metrics.description: A conceptual innovation can generate a vast range of solvable problems (e.g., Dalton's atomic conception enabled systematic chemical measurement), producing rapid convergence across a community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a conceptual shift changed the structure of relevant problem space and enabled new empirical or measurement practices leading to consensus; look for downstream standardization of techniques (e.g., measurement improvements) as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple independent discovery as evidence of historical robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: The routine occurrence of multiple discoveries indicates that some end-states (theories, practices) are historically robust or 'virtually inevitable' given the range of possibilities and causal factors affecting development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use instances of multiple, independent discovery to infer attractor-like states in 'practice space' (analogous to phenotypic optima); Merton's discussion of genius as arriving early at points that others reach later is cited as supportive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Path-independence / attractor status of certain practice-space points
rubrics_metrics.description: Some points in practice space are more or less inevitable because they maximize a kind of scientific 'fitness' (fruitfulness); whether the community reaches them may be path-independent in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate candidate attractors by asking whether diverse historical paths converge on similar solutions and whether those solutions generate sustained, fruitful research programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heredity and intrinsicity criteria for approximating a Darwinian population
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific practice must satisfy certain constraints (e.g., heredity, intrinsicity) to approximate a paradigmatically Darwinian population; earlier chapters argue that science often appears to satisfy the heredity criterion and the intrinsicity condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether natural selection plausibly modifies scientific practice, check for (a) mechanisms by which successful practices/knowledge are reliably transmitted (heredity) and (b) that variation and selection operate on factors intrinsic to the epistemic population (intrinsicity). The page references these criteria as measures of natural selection's effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testability via multiple independent implications
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid vague analogy, derive a set of predictions that should be visible in the historical record if the causal model is correct, and check whether those expectations are realized across independent lines of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an array of independent qualitative expectations (not just a single match) to lower chance of coincidental fits; require historical accountability and concrete empirical checks rather than loose resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between historical detail and explanatory abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective historical explanation must strike the right balance between too-fine-grained historical detail and explanatory abstraction; looking at too fine-grained a level can obscure genuine causal patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating explanatory claims, ensure the scale and granularity of analysis permit detection of patterns: neither so coarse as to be vacuous, nor so fine as to lose generalizable causal structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish substantive explanatory abstractions from vague/plastic ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid models with 'excessive plasticity' (Kuhn's worry) that are so loose they can be made to fit almost anything; explanatory abstractions should be substantive and empirically accountable rather than vague.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should test whether the purported generalizations produce concrete, falsifiable implications and whether alternative explanations are genuinely ruled out; check whether the model's constraints (e.g., Godfrey-Smith's) meaningfully limit application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical trends (growth) as epistemic constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical trends—such as the growth (increasing breadth) of scientific knowledge—are epistemologically significant and can function as constraints that viable theories of knowledge must obey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating normative or theoretical accounts of knowledge, include large-scale historical trends (community-level, long timescales) as evidential constraints; the page lists at least four reasons for the epistemic significance of growth and treats them as legitimate constraints on theories.
